changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
changes.change: For buyers who come in with a failure problem, don't lead with an average. Use their own dashboard figure and say what it costs them: 'You told us about one in twelve online orders is failing at the payment step, and it's worse on the big baskets. Here's what those orders are worth to you each month, and how many we expect to recover.' Back it with an estimate built from their decline export, and keep the 'why big orders get knocked back' explanation as the lead story.
changes.why: We showed 'the uplift slide. The average improvement in acceptance.', but the champion responded to the decline explanation and had a failure rate from her own dashboard, so an estimate built on her numbers is sharper than an average about other customers.

changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
changes.change: When a finance approver signs off and won't take vendor meetings, make the ROI proof a one-page business case in the customer's own numbers that the champion can hand straight to the CFO. It should show the value of failed orders recovered (from a three-month decline export) against the rate difference, plus any other costs the customer confirms. Offer it before the pricing proposal goes out: 'Here's a one-page business case you can hand your CFO, built on your numbers.'
changes.why: The champion asked for 'something she could hand Martin. Like a one-page business case' and got a deck and pricing proposal, while the controller's one-pager the CFO actually read compared only rates.

changes.change: Add a response for when the incumbent counters on rate: 'A lower rate on orders that still fail at the last step isn't cheaper. Here's the rate difference next to what your failed orders are worth.' This puts revenue lost per failed order beside the rate gap, so the comparison isn't 'the same thing' at a different price.
changes.why: Once the bank 'came back and sharpened the rate', 'every email was the rate' even though Lucy had been asking about declines, and the CFO read the result as 'Why would I pay more for the same thing'.

changes.change: For ecommerce leads, write acceptance copy in the buyer's words rather than 'authorization rates': 'Stop orders dying at the last step, especially the big baskets. You do all the work to get someone to buy, then the card says no.' Pair each line with a money figure a CFO can read.
changes.why: The champion framed the problem as 'orders dying at the last step', 'the big baskets' and 'the card says no', which is sharper and more about revenue than our acceptance language.
